<!-- maintheorem-1: body_md -->
Let $p,q\geq 2$ and $g,h\geq 2$, and suppose
\[
p(g-1)=q(h-1)=n.
\]
A direct cyclic mixed sum can have the rational cohomology ring of $\#_k(S^2\times S^2)$ only when $k$ is odd.  For odd $k$, put $t=(k+1)/2$, $a=g-1$, and $b=h-1$.  Then the numerical types are exactly the solutions of
\[
n=a+b+t,\qquad a\mid b+t,\qquad b\mid a+t.
\]
For every such type there is a minimal equatorially product-framed symplectic realization $Z$ with
\[
H^*(Z;\mathbb Q)\cong H^*(\#_k(S^2\times S^2);\mathbb Q).
\]
After a possibly different choice of spin-compatible symplectic normal framings, the type also admits a spin realization, product-framed relative to those framings, for which $Q_{Z,\mathrm{free}}\cong kH$.  For every direct gluing,
\[
\pi_1(\Sigma_G)\times\mathbb Z\hookrightarrow\pi_1(Z).
\]
<!-- end maintheorem-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:multi}
The surface $F_{g,p}$ is connected, embedded, and symplectic.  The projection $F_{g,p}\to \Sigma_g$ is an unbranched cyclic cover of degree $p$, and
\[
[F_{g,p}]=p[\Sigma_g\times\{\mathrm{pt}\}],\qquad F_{g,p}^2=0,
\]
while
\[
g(F_{g,p})=p(g-1)+1.
\]
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
The equation $z^p=u(x)$ is the pullback of the standard degree-$p$ covering $S^1\to S^1$.  Since $z\mapsto z^p$ is a local diffeomorphism, the fiber product is a smooth embedded surface even over critical points of $u$.  Primitivity of $\xi$ makes the induced character onto $\mathbb Z/p$, hence the pullback cover is connected.  If
\[
[F_{g,p}]=a[\Sigma_g\times\{\mathrm{pt}\}]+b[\{\mathrm{pt}\}\times S^2],
\]
intersection with a sphere fiber gives $a=p$, while intersection with a section whose $S^2$-coordinate is disjoint from the equator gives $b=0$.  Thus $[F_{g,p}]=p[\Sigma_g\times\{\mathrm{pt}\}]$ and $F_{g,p}^2=0$.  The genus formula is Riemann--Hurwitz for an unbranched cover.  For a product symplectic form, the vertical component of the tangent plane lies in the one-dimensional tangent space of the equator.  The $S^2$-area term therefore restricts trivially, while the pullback of the area form on the base is positive.  Hence $F_{g,p}$ is symplectic.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:geo}
The mixed sum satisfies
\[
e(Z^{p,q}_{g,h})=4n\left(1-\frac1p-\frac1q\right),\qquad
\sigma(Z^{p,q}_{g,h})=0.
\]
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Since $g=1+n/p$, $h=1+n/q$, and $e(\Sigma_G)=2-2G=-2n$, the fiber-sum formula gives
\begin{align*}
e(Z)&=(4-4g)+(4-4h)-2(2-2G)\\
&=4n\left(1-\frac1p-\frac1q\right).
\end{align*}
Both product ruled surfaces have signature zero, so Novikov additivity gives $\sigma(Z)=0$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:classification}
Assume $k\geq1$, $p,q\geq 2$, $g,h\geq 2$, and \eqref{eq:n}.  Suppose that a mixed sum has the rational cohomology ring of $\#_k(S^2\times S^2)$.  Then $k$ is odd.  Put
\[
t=\frac{k+1}{2},\qquad a=g-1,\qquad b=h-1.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:class}
n=a+b+t,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:div}
a\mid b+t,\qquad b\mid a+t.
\end{equation}
Conversely, every pair of positive integers $(a,b)$ satisfying \eqref{eq:div}, with $n$ defined by \eqref{eq:class}, determines integers
\[
p=\frac na,\qquad q=\frac nb,
\]
with $p,q\geq 2$, and the resulting mixed sum has
\[
e=2+2k,\qquad \sigma=0.
\]
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The connected sum $\#_k(S^2\times S^2)$ has Euler characteristic $2+2k$ and signature zero.  Proposition~\ref{prop:geo} therefore gives
\[
4n\left(1-\frac1p-\frac1q\right)=2+2k.
\]
Since
\[
n\left(1-\frac1p-\frac1q\right)=n-a-b\in\mathbb Z,
\]
the left side is divisible by four.  Thus $2+2k$ is divisible by four and $k$ is odd.  Writing $t=(k+1)/2$ gives
\[
n-\frac np-\frac nq=t.
\]
Since $a=n/p$ and $b=n/q$, this is exactly \eqref{eq:class}.  The conditions $p,q\in\mathbb Z$ are equivalent to $a\mid n$ and $b\mid n$.  Using $n=a+b+t$, these become \eqref{eq:div}.

Conversely, if \eqref{eq:div} holds, then $a\mid n$ and $b\mid n$, so $p=n/a$ and $q=n/b$ are integers.  Since $n>a,b$, both are at least two.  Substitution in Proposition~\ref{prop:geo} gives $e=4t=2+2k$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:param}
Fix $t\geq 1$.  Up to interchanging the two summands, assume $a\leq b$ and write
\[
b=a+d,\qquad d\geq 0.
\]
Then $0\leq d\leq t$.  If $0\leq d<t$, all solutions are obtained by choosing $a>0$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:param1}
a\mid t+d,\qquad a+d\mid t-d.
\end{equation}
If $d=t$, all solutions are obtained by choosing
\begin{equation}\label{eq:param2}
a\mid 2t,
\end{equation}
and setting $b=a+t$.
In particular, for each fixed odd $k$ there are only finitely many numerical mixed-sum types.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
From \eqref{eq:div}, with $b=a+d$, we have
\[
a\mid d+t
\]
and
\[
a+d\mid a+t.
\]
Subtracting $a+d$ from the second dividend gives
\[
a+d\mid t-d.
\]
If $d>t$, then $0<d-t<a+d$, so this divisibility is impossible.  Thus $d\leq t$.

If $d<t$, the two divisibility conditions are exactly \eqref{eq:param1}.  If $d=t$, the second condition is automatic and the first becomes $a\mid 2t$.  These conditions are also sufficient by reversing the calculation.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:degrees}
For $d<t$ one may write the corresponding degrees directly as
\[
p=2+\frac{t+d}{a},\qquad
q=2+\frac{t-d}{a+d}.
\]
For $d=t$ one has
\[
p=2+\frac{2t}{a},\qquad q=2.
\]
Thus, for $d<t$, the solutions are generated from the indicated divisor conditions involving $t-d$ and $t+d$; for $d=t$, they are generated by the positive divisors of $2t$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:counts}
For $k=1,3,5,7,9,11,13,15$, the numbers of unordered numerical types are respectively
\[
3,5,7,7,9,11,10,10.
\]
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:param} for $t=1,\ldots,8$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:covermap}
For the degree-$p$ covering $q:F_{g,p}\to\Sigma_g$, the map
\[
Q_{p,g}=q_*:H_1(F_{g,p};\mathbb Q)\longrightarrow H_1(\Sigma_g;\mathbb Q)
\]
is surjective.  Its kernel is a symplectic subspace of dimension $2G-2g$ in $H_1(F_{g,p};\mathbb Q)$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
The transfer, or equivalently the pullback on homology after identifying homology and cohomology by Poincar\'e duality, gives a map $q^!$ satisfying
\[
q_*q^!=p\,\mathrm{id}.
\]
Hence $q_*$ is surjective over $\mathbb Q$.  Moreover $q_*$ and $q^!$ are adjoint for the algebraic intersection pairings.  Thus
\[
\ker q_*=(\operatorname{im}q^!)^\perp.
\]
The restriction of the intersection form to $\operatorname{im}q^!$ is $p$ times the intersection form downstairs and is therefore nondegenerate.  Its symplectic orthogonal complement is consequently nondegenerate as well.  The dimension statement follows from surjectivity.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:integralimage}
Choose a symplectic basis $a_1,b_1,\ldots,a_g,b_g$ so that the covering
character sends $a_1$ to $1\in\mathbb Z/p$ and the other basis elements to
zero.  Then
\[
\operatorname{im}\bigl(q_*:H_1(F_{g,p};\mathbb Z)\to
H_1(\Sigma_g;\mathbb Z)\bigr)
=\langle pa_1,b_1,a_2,b_2,\ldots,a_g,b_g\rangle.
\]
In particular, this image is the kernel of the covering character on
$H_1(\Sigma_g;\mathbb Z)$ and its cokernel is $\mathbb Z/p$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Every closed loop upstairs projects to a loop in the kernel of the covering
character.  Conversely, the curves representing $b_1,a_i,b_i$ for $i\geq2$
lift to closed curves, as does the $p$-fold traversal of $a_1$.  Their homology
classes generate the displayed kernel, which proves the assertion.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:sympposition}
Let $V$ be a symplectic vector space of dimension $2G$, and let
$K_1,K_2\subset V$ be symplectic subspaces of dimensions $r$ and $s$.
There is a symplectic automorphism $T$ such that
\[
\dim(K_1\cap T^{-1}K_2)=\max\{0,r+s-2G\}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Use the symplectic orthogonal decomposition
\[
V=K_1\oplus K_1^\perp.
\]
If $s\leq 2G-r$, choose a symplectic subspace $K_2'\subset K_1^\perp$
of dimension $s$; then $K_1\cap K_2'=0$.  If $s>2G-r$, choose a
symplectic subspace $L\subset K_1$ of dimension $s-(2G-r)$ and put
\[
K_2'=K_1^\perp\oplus L.
\]
Then $K_2'$ is symplectic of dimension $s$ and
\[
\dim(K_1\cap K_2')=s-(2G-r)=r+s-2G.
\]
Every two symplectic subspaces of the same dimension are carried to one
another by a symplectic automorphism.  Choose one carrying $K_2'$ to
$K_2$, and take its inverse for $T$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:gap}
For every numerical type in Theorem~\ref{thm:classification},
\[
G-g-h=t-1=\frac{k-1}{2}.
\]
In particular, $G\geq g+h$, with equality exactly when $k=1$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Using $G=n+1$, $g=a+1$, $h=b+1$, and $n=a+b+t$ gives
\[
G-g-h=(a+b+t+1)-(a+b+2)=t-1.
\]
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:existence}
Every numerical type in Theorem~\ref{thm:classification} admits an equatorially product-framed symplectic gluing $\varphi$ for which
\[
H_1(Z^{p,q}_{g,h}(\varphi);\mathbb Q)=0.
\]
Consequently
\[
H^*(Z^{p,q}_{g,h}(\varphi);\mathbb Q)
\cong
H^*(\#_k(S^2\times S^2);\mathbb Q)
\]
as graded rings.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:covermap},
\[
K_A=\ker A,\qquad K_B=\ker B
\]
are symplectic subspaces of $V$, of dimensions
\[
2G-2g,\qquad 2G-2h.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:sympposition} gives $T\in\operatorname{Sp}(V)$ for which
\[
\dim(K_A\cap T^{-1}K_B)
=
\max\{0,2G-2g-2h\}.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:gap}, $G\geq g+h$, and therefore
\[
\dim(K_A\cap T^{-1}K_B)=2G-2g-2h.
\]
It follows that
\[
\operatorname{rk}\Theta_T=2g+2h,
\]
so $\Theta_T$ is onto.
Indeed,
\[
\ker\Theta_T=K_A\cap T^{-1}K_B,
\]
and therefore
\[
\operatorname{rk}\Theta_T=2G-(2G-2g-2h)=2g+2h,
\]
the dimension of the target.

The maximal-rank condition is the nonvanishing of at least one $(2g+2h)\times(2g+2h)$ minor.  Hence it is a nonempty Zariski-open condition on the symplectic group.  Since $\operatorname{Sp}(2G,\mathbb Z)$ is Zariski dense in $\operatorname{Sp}(2G,\mathbb R)$ \cite{Borel}, an integral symplectic matrix can be chosen.  The mapping class group of $\Sigma_G$ surjects onto $\operatorname{Sp}(2G,\mathbb Z)$ \cite{FarbMargalit}, so this matrix is realized by a gluing diffeomorphism.  The two induced area forms on $\Sigma_G$ have the same total area.  By Moser's theorem the diffeomorphism may be isotoped, without changing its action on homology, so that it preserves the area form.  Together with the reversal of the normal circle, it therefore gives a symplectic sum gluing.

Over $\mathbb Q$ the meridional torsion in \eqref{eq:H1comp} vanishes.  Surjectivity of $\Theta_T$ therefore gives $H_1(Z;\mathbb Q)=0$.  Since
\[
e(Z)=2+2k,\qquad \sigma(Z)=0,
\]
we obtain
\[
b_2(Z)=2k,\qquad b_2^+(Z)=b_2^-(Z)=k.
\]
The integral intersection pairing on $H_2(Z;\mathbb Z)/\operatorname{Tor}$ is unimodular of rank $2k$ and signature zero.  If it is odd, the classification of indefinite odd unimodular forms gives $k\langle1\rangle\oplus k\langle-1\rangle$; if it is even, the indefinite even unimodular form of signature $(k,k)$ is $kH$; see \cite[Chapter~II, Sections~4--5]{MilnorHusemoller}.  After tensoring with $\mathbb Q$, both forms are isometric to $kH$: for one pair $\langle1\rangle\oplus\langle-1\rangle$ with basis $e,f$, the vectors $e+f$ and $(e-f)/2$ form a hyperbolic pair.  Poincar\'e duality gives $H_3(Z;\mathbb Q)\cong H_1(Z;\mathbb Q)=0$, and for a closed oriented four-manifold with $b_1=0$ the graded rational cohomology ring is determined by its intersection pairing.  This proves the stated ring isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
For $k=1$ the map $\Theta_T$ is square.  For $k>1$ it is rectangular, with
\[
\dim V-(2g+2h)=k-1.
\]
Thus the determinant used in the smallest case is replaced by maximal minors.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:boundarymap}
With the equatorial framing, the inclusion
\(F_{g,p}\times S^1\hookrightarrow M_{g,p}\) induces
\[
 (v,r)\longmapsto (Q_{p,g}v,r\mu_p)
\]
under the splitting \eqref{eq:H1comp}.  Replacing the framing by a map
\(\lambda:H_1(F_{g,p};\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z\) changes only the
meridional component, replacing \(r\) by \(r+\lambda(v)\).
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The projection of a boundary surface loop to the base is the covering
push-forward \(Q_{p,g}\).  In the equatorial trivialization its normal
coordinate is constant, so it has no meridional component.  More
geometrically, choose along the equator the unit normal vector field in
$S^2$ orthogonal to the equator.  Pushing a loop of $F_{g,p}$ in this
direction keeps it on one fixed side of the multisection, and the resulting
push-off has zero meridional coordinate, equivalently zero linking in the
cyclic meridian group $\mathbb Z/p$.  Thus its class has no component along
the meridian.  The normal circle bounds a normal disk in $\nu F_{g,p}$
and represents the peripheral loop \(\mu_p\) in the punctured-sphere
fiber of the complement.  Twisting the
normal trivialization along a loop \(v\) adds \(\lambda(v)\) turns around
that peripheral loop, which gives the last assertion.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:MV}
With rows ordered as
\[
H_1(\Sigma_g;\mathbb Z)\oplus\mathbb Z\langle\mu_p\rangle
\oplus H_1(\Sigma_h;\mathbb Z)\oplus\mathbb Z\langle\mu_q\rangle
\]
and columns ordered as
\[
H_1(\Sigma_G;\mathbb Z)\oplus\mathbb Z\langle r\rangle
\oplus\mathbb Z\langle\rho_p\rangle\oplus\mathbb Z\langle\rho_q\rangle,
\]
where $r$ is the common normal-circle generator and $\rho_p,\rho_q$
record the two meridional torsion relations, the first homology of the
mixed sum is the cokernel of
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
Q_{p,g}&0&0&0\\
0&1&p&0\\
-Q_{q,h}S&0&0&0\\
-\lambda&1&0&q
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Equivalently, if $d=\gcd(p,q)$, it is the cokernel of the homomorphism
\[
H_1(\Sigma_G;\mathbb Z)\oplus\mathbb Z
\longrightarrow
H_1(\Sigma_g;\mathbb Z)\oplus H_1(\Sigma_h;\mathbb Z)\oplus\mathbb Z
\]
represented by
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
Q_{p,g}&0\\
-Q_{q,h}S&0\\
\lambda&d
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
For a product-framed gluing, $\lambda=0$, and
\[
H_1(Z;\mathbb Z)\cong
\operatorname{coker}\begin{pmatrix}Q_{p,g}\\-Q_{q,h}S\end{pmatrix}
\oplus \mathbb Z/d.
\]
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The boundary and the two complements are connected, so the map on
$H_0$ in the Mayer--Vietoris sequence is injective.  Hence $H_1(Z)$ is
the cokernel of the boundary map on $H_1$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:boundarymap}, the Mayer--Vietoris map on the boundary
surface and normal-circle generators is
\[
(v,r)\longmapsto
\bigl(Q_{p,g}v,r\mu_p,-Q_{q,h}Sv,
(r-\lambda(v))\mu_q\bigr),
\]
up to simultaneously changing the signs in one summand.  Adjoining the
two torsion relations gives the displayed four-block presentation from the
two splittings
\[
H_1(M_{g,p};\mathbb Z)=H_1(\Sigma_g;\mathbb Z)\oplus \mathbb Z/p,
\]
\[
H_1(M_{h,q};\mathbb Z)=H_1(\Sigma_h;\mathbb Z)\oplus \mathbb Z/q.
\]
The column containing the common normal circle gives
$\mu_p+\mu_q=0$.  Substituting $\mu_q=-\mu_p$ changes the entry
$-\lambda$ in the last row to $+\lambda$ in the reduced meridional row;
equivalently, this is an allowed integral sign operation followed by
elimination of the common normal-circle column.  The two remaining relations
\(p\mu=0\) and \(q\mu=0\) are equivalent, by integral elementary
operations, to \(d\mu=0\), where \(d=\gcd(p,q)\).  This yields the reduced
presentation.  When \(\lambda=0\), the meridional row is independent of
the surface rows and splits off as \(\mathbb Z/d\).
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:quotients}
Every direct mixed sum has quotients $\mathbb Z/p$ and $\mathbb Z/q$ in first homology.  In particular, no direct mixed sum in this paper is simply connected or has the integral homology of $\#_k(S^2\times S^2)$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:integralimage}, the image of $H_1(F_{g,p};\mathbb Z)$ in the base homology is the kernel of the covering character
\[
H_1(\Sigma_g;\mathbb Z)\to \mathbb Z/p.
\]
Project the target of the Mayer--Vietoris map to
\[
H_1(\Sigma_g;\mathbb Z)/\operatorname{im}Q_{p,g}\cong\mathbb Z/p
\]
and send the second summand and both meridional classes to zero.  Every
boundary relation, including the framing term, maps to zero, so the map
descends to a surjection from \(H_1(Z;\mathbb Z)\).  Reversing the roles of
the two sides gives the quotient \(\mathbb Z/q\).
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:productcover}
Let $q:F_{g,p}\to\Sigma_g$ be the explicit cyclic multisection cover of
Proposition~\ref{prop:multi}.  The pullback of the complement bundle admits
a natural fiberwise trivialization after the defining root coordinate and
equivariant tubular neighborhoods are fixed:
\[
q^*M_{g,p}\cong F_{g,p}\times P_p.
\]
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
A point of $F_{g,p}$ is a pair $(x,z)$ with $z^p=u(x)$.  Over $x$, the
punctures of the sphere fiber are the points
\[
z,\zeta z,\ldots,\zeta^{p-1}z,
\qquad \zeta=e^{2\pi i/p},
\]
on the equator.  Rotation of the sphere by multiplication with $z^{-1}$
fixes the two poles and carries this configuration to the fixed set of
$p$th roots of unity.  These rotations vary smoothly with $(x,z)$ and,
after choosing equivariant tubular disks around the punctures, give a
fiber-preserving diffeomorphism from the pullback complement to
$F_{g,p}\times P_p$.  Thus no residual pure braid or point-pushing
monodromy remains in this explicit root construction.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:incomp}
For the explicit cyclic equatorial multisection
$F_{g,p}\subset\Sigma_g\times S^2$ of degree $p\geq2$, the homomorphism
\[
\pi_1(\partial\nu F_{g,p})\longrightarrow \pi_1(M_{g,p})
\]
is injective.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Let $\chi:\pi_1(\Sigma_g)\to\mathbb Z/p$ be the covering character and
pull $M_{g,p}$ back to the corresponding cover.  By
Lemma~\ref{lem:productcover}, the resulting complement cover is
$F_{g,p}\times P_p$.  The character defining this cover is trivial on
the boundary group: $q_*$ is injective,
$q_*\pi_1(F_{g,p})=\ker\chi$, and the normal circle is vertical.  More
explicitly, the pullback of the boundary is
\[
F_{g,p}\times_{\Sigma_g}F_{g,p}\times S^1.
\]
Since $q$ is a regular cyclic cover, the fiber product is the disjoint
union of the graphs of its $p$ deck transformations.  Thus each lifted
boundary component is naturally $F_{g,p}\times S^1$ and maps
homeomorphically to the original boundary.
For such a component the inclusion is
\[
\pi_1(F_{g,p})\times\mathbb Z\longrightarrow
\pi_1(F_{g,p})\times\pi_1(P_p),
\]
and is injective because a boundary circle of $P_p$ is incompressible for
$p\geq2$.  If a boundary loop is null-homotopic in $M_{g,p}$, its closed
lift to this boundary component has a lifted null-homotopy in the product
cover.  Injectivity upstairs makes the lifted loop trivial.  Since the
chosen boundary component maps homeomorphically to the original one, the
original loop is trivial as well.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:pi1}
For every direct mixed sum in Theorem~\ref{thm:classification},
\[
\pi_1(\Sigma_G)\times\mathbb Z\hookrightarrow \pi_1(Z).
\]
Consequently $\pi_1(Z)$ is nontrivial and contains $\mathbb Z^2$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Van Kampen identifies the group with an amalgamated product of the two complement groups over the common boundary group.  By Theorem~\ref{thm:incomp}, both boundary maps are injective, and the normal form theorem for amalgamated products injects the boundary group into the final group.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:bassserre}
For every direct mixed sum, $\pi_1(Z)$ acts without inversion on a Bass--Serre tree $T$ whose quotient is a single edge.  The two vertex stabilizers are conjugate to $\pi_1(M_{g,p})$ and $\pi_1(M_{h,q})$, and the edge stabilizer is conjugate to $\pi_1(\Sigma_G)\times\mathbb Z$.  Moreover, writing $F_r$ for the free group of rank $r$,
\[
\pi_1(M_{g,p})\text{ contains an index-}p\text{ subgroup }\pi_1(\Sigma_G)\times F_{p-1},
\]
and similarly $\pi_1(M_{h,q})$ contains an index-$q$ subgroup $\pi_1(\Sigma_G)\times F_{q-1}$.  The splitting is nontrivial.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Van Kampen and Theorem~\ref{thm:incomp} give
\[
\pi_1(Z)\cong
\pi_1(M_{g,p})*_{\pi_1(\Sigma_G)\times\mathbb Z}\pi_1(M_{h,q}).
\]
This gives the Bass--Serre action and the stabilizers.  Lemma~\ref{lem:productcover} identifies the pullback of $M_{g,p}\to\Sigma_g$ by the cyclic cover $\Sigma_G\to\Sigma_g$ with $\Sigma_G\times P_p$.  Hence the corresponding index-$p$ subgroup is
\[
\pi_1(\Sigma_G)\times\pi_1(P_p)=\pi_1(\Sigma_G)\times F_{p-1}.
\]
The same argument applies on the other side.  Finally, each boundary
inclusion is proper.  On the first side, projection to the base quotient
gives
\[
H_1(M_{g,p};\mathbb Z)/\operatorname{im}H_1(\partial M_{g,p};\mathbb Z)
\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb Z/p,
\]
and the analogous quotient on the second side surjects onto \(\mathbb Z/q\).
Thus neither vertex group equals the edge group, and the splitting is
nontrivial.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:centralizer}
Let $\Gamma<\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)\times\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)$.  Suppose that $\Gamma$ contains a subgroup $H\times\langle z\rangle$, where $H$ is a nonabelian surface group and $z$ has infinite order.  If both projections of $z$ to the two factors are nontrivial, then this is impossible.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Write $z=(z_1,z_2)$.  Since $z$ centralizes $H$, the image of $H$ lies in
\[
C_{\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)}(z_1)\times C_{\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)}(z_2).
\]
The centralizer of a nonidentity element of $\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)$ is abelian.  Indeed, according as the element is hyperbolic, parabolic, or elliptic, its centralizer is conjugate to a one-parameter diagonal subgroup, a one-parameter unipotent subgroup, or the rotation subgroup.  If both $z_1$ and $z_2$ are nontrivial, the displayed product is abelian, contradicting the fact that $H$ is nonabelian.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:lattice}
Let $Z$ be a direct mixed sum formed from the explicit cyclic equatorial
multisections of Section~2.  Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
\item $\pi_1(Z)$ is not word-hyperbolic;
\item $\pi_1(Z)$ is not a cocompact lattice in $\operatorname{PO}(n,1)$ for any $n\geq2$;
\item $\pi_1(Z)$ is not a cocompact lattice in $\operatorname{PU}(n,1)$ for any $n\geq2$;
\item $\pi_1(Z)$ is not a torsion-free cocompact irreducible lattice in $\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)\times\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, it is not a cocompact Deligne--Mostow lattice in $\operatorname{PU}(2,1)$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
By Corollary~\ref{cor:pi1}, the group $\pi_1(Z)$ contains
$\pi_1(\Sigma_G)\times\mathbb Z$, and hence contains $\mathbb Z^2$.
Every abelian subgroup of a word-hyperbolic group is virtually cyclic.
It follows that $\pi_1(Z)$ is not word-hyperbolic, proving (1).

Let $X$ be either real hyperbolic $n$-space or complex hyperbolic
$n$-space.  A cocompact lattice in $\operatorname{Isom}(X)$ acts properly
and cocompactly on $X$.  By the Milnor--\v{S}varc lemma it is
quasi-isometric to $X$, and is therefore word-hyperbolic because $X$ is a
proper geodesic Gromov-hyperbolic space; see \cite{BridsonHaefliger}.
Thus (1) implies (2) and (3).

For (4), suppose that $\pi_1(Z)$ is isomorphic to a torsion-free
cocompact irreducible lattice
\[
\Gamma<\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)\times
\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R).
\]
Let $\operatorname{pr}_i$ denote projection to the $i$th factor.  By
irreducibility, both $\operatorname{pr}_1(\Gamma)$ and
$\operatorname{pr}_2(\Gamma)$ are dense.  Set
\[
K_1=\Gamma\cap
\bigl(\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)\times\{1\}\bigr).
\]
Then $K_1$ is discrete and normal in $\Gamma$.  Its projection to the
first factor is normalized by the dense subgroup
$\operatorname{pr}_1(\Gamma)$.  Since the normalizer of a closed subgroup
is closed, $\operatorname{pr}_1(K_1)$ is normal in all of
$\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)$.  It is therefore a discrete normal
subgroup of the connected center-free simple group
$\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)$, and hence is trivial.  Thus $K_1$ is
trivial.  The same argument for the other factor shows that both
coordinate projections are injective on $\Gamma$.

Under the assumed isomorphism, Corollary~\ref{cor:pi1} gives a subgroup
$\pi_1(\Sigma_G)\times\langle z\rangle$ of $\Gamma$, where $z$ has
infinite order.  Here $G=p(g-1)+1\geq3$, so $\pi_1(\Sigma_G)$ is
nonabelian.  The injectivity of the two coordinate projections implies
that both coordinates of $z$ are nontrivial, contradicting
Lemma~\ref{lem:centralizer}.  This proves (4).  Finally, any
Deligne--Mostow lattice in $\operatorname{PU}(2,1)$ is a
complex-hyperbolic lattice, so its cocompact instances are excluded by
(3) \cite{DeligneMostow}.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:triangletypes}
Let $k=2t-1$ and suppose that $t\mid n$.  Put $r=n/t$.  Up to
interchanging $p$ and $q$, the numerical types satisfying
\[
\frac1p+\frac1q+\frac1r=1
\]
are exactly the following:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
(p,q,r)&n&(g-1,h-1)&\text{condition}\ \\ \hline
(3,3,3)&3t&(t,t)&\text{all }t\\
(4,2,4)&4t&(t,2t)&\text{all }t\\
(4,4,2)&2t&(t/2,t/2)&2\mid t\\
(3,2,6)&6t&(2t,3t)&\text{all }t\\
(6,2,3)&3t&(t/2,3t/2)&2\mid t\\
(6,3,2)&2t&(t/3,2t/3)&3\mid t.
\end{array}
\]
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
The classification equation may be written as
\[
\frac1p+\frac1q+\frac{t}{n}=1.
\]
Whenever $t\mid n$, write $n=tr$.  Then
\[
\frac1p+\frac1q+\frac1r=1.
\]
Since $p,q,r\geq2$, the triple $(p,q,r)$ is a permutation of
\[
(2,3,6),\qquad (2,4,4),\qquad (3,3,3).
\]
After ordering the three integers, the smallest is at most three; the
cases two and three give exactly the triples above.  Since $r$ is
distinguished, placing it in each of the possible positions gives the six
rows of the table.  A placement gives a numerical type precisely when
\[
g-1=\frac{tr}{p},\qquad h-1=\frac{tr}{q}
\]
are integers.  These are exactly the divisibility conditions displayed
in the last column.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:min}
Every symplectic direct mixed sum considered in this paper is symplectically minimal.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Each summand $\Sigma_g\times S^2$, with $g\geq 2$, is a minimal ruled surface.  The gluing surface $F_{g,p}$ has genus
\[
p(g-1)+1>g
\]
for $p\geq 2$.  It cannot be a section of a ruling, since a section has the genus of the base.  Usher's minimality theorem for symplectic sums \cite{Usher} therefore applies.  Indeed, neither summand contains an exceptional sphere, and the ruled exception in Usher's theorem occurs only when the sum surface is a section.  Both exceptional alternatives are absent.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
Every rational-cohomology example of Theorem~\ref{thm:existence} has symplectic Kodaira dimension two.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
The examples are minimal.  They are not rational, since rational
four-manifolds are simply connected whereas Corollary~\ref{cor:pi1}
gives a nontrivial fundamental group containing $\mathbb Z^2$.  They are
not ruled over a positive-genus surface, since such a ruled manifold has
positive first Betti number whereas $b_1(Z)=0$.  They have
\[
K_\omega^2=2e+3\sigma=4(k+1)>0.
\]
Since the manifold is minimal, nonrational, and nonruled, the main theorem of Liu \cite{Liu}, together with $K_\omega^2>0$, gives $K_\omega\cdot[\omega]>0$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:spinpull}
Let $q:\Sigma_G\to\Sigma_g$ be a connected cyclic covering of degree $p$
defined by a character of exact order $p$.
As the spin structure $s$ on $\Sigma_g$ varies, both Arf invariants occur
among the pullbacks $q^*s$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Choose a complex structure downstairs and lift it to the cover.  Represent
$s$ by a theta characteristic $L$.  If $A$ is the flat line bundle of
exact order $p$ defining the cyclic cover, then, up to replacing $A$ by
its inverse,
\[
q_*\mathcal O_{\Sigma_G}=\bigoplus_{j=0}^{p-1}A^j.
\]
The projection formula gives
\[
h^0(\Sigma_G,q^*L)=\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}h^0(\Sigma_g,L\otimes A^j).
\]
Serre duality, Riemann--Roch, and $L^2=K$ identify modulo two the terms
indexed by $j$ and $-j$.
They therefore cancel in pairs modulo two.  If $p$ is odd, only the
trivial character remains, and Atiyah's mod-two index theorem
\cite{AtiyahSpin} gives
\[
\operatorname{Arf}(q^*s)=\operatorname{Arf}(s).
\]
Both values occur among spin structures on $\Sigma_g$.

Suppose that $p$ is even.  The two unpaired characters are the trivial
character and the nontrivial order-two character $\eta=A^{p/2}$.  We also write
$\eta$ for the corresponding nonzero class in
$H^1(\Sigma_g;\mathbb Z/2)$.  If $q_s$ is the
quadratic refinement associated to $s$, then
\[
q_s(\operatorname{PD}\eta)
\equiv h^0(\Sigma_g,L\otimes\eta)+h^0(\Sigma_g,L)\pmod2;
\]
this is the theta-characteristic definition of the quadratic refinement
\cite{MumfordTheta}.  The projection formula and the cancellation of the
paired characters therefore give
\[
\operatorname{Arf}(q^*s)=q_s(\operatorname{PD}\eta).
\]
For $\alpha\in H^1(\Sigma_g;\mathbb Z/2)$,
\[
q_{s+\alpha}(\operatorname{PD}\eta)
=q_s(\operatorname{PD}\eta)
+\langle\alpha\smile\eta,[\Sigma_g]\rangle.
\]
Since $\eta\ne0$ and the intersection pairing is nondegenerate, the last
term takes both values.  Hence both pullback parities occur.  The mod-two
index is topological, so the result is independent of the auxiliary
complex structure.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:spinframing}
Let $X$ be an oriented spin four-manifold and let $F\subset X$ be an
oriented embedded surface with trivial oriented normal bundle.  Given a
spin structure $s_F$ on $F$, there is an oriented normal framing for which
the spin structure induced on $TF$ from
\[
TX|_F=TF\oplus\nu F
\]
is $s_F$.  In the corresponding tubular coordinates the boundary spin
structure on $F\times S^1$ is
$s_F\boxtimes s_{\mathrm{bnd}}$, where $s_{\mathrm{bnd}}$ is the
bounding spin structure on the circle.  If $F$ is symplectic and
$F^2=0$, the framing may be chosen symplectic.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Start with a normal framing inducing a spin structure $s_0$ on $F$.  The
difference $s_F-s_0$ is a class $\delta\in H^1(F;\mathbb Z/2)$.  The
reduction map $H^1(F;\mathbb Z)\to H^1(F;\mathbb Z/2)$ is onto.  Choose
an integral lift of $\delta$ and represent it by a map $F\to SO(2)$.
Twisting the framing by this map changes the induced tangential spin
structure by $\delta$.  The spin structure on the normal disk restricts
to the bounding spin structure on its boundary.  In the symplectic case
the same twist lies in $SO(2)=U(1)$ and preserves the symplectic normal
trivialization.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:spin}
For every numerical type in Theorem~\ref{thm:classification}, there are
spin-compatible symplectic normal framings and a product gluing relative
to those framings such that
\[
H_1(Z;\mathbb Q)=0,\qquad w_2(Z)=0.
\]
For such a gluing,
\[
Q_{Z,\mathrm{free}}\cong kH.
\]
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Choose spin structures $s_g$ and $s_h$ on the base surfaces so that their
pullbacks to $\Sigma_G$ have the same Arf invariant.  This is possible by
Lemma~\ref{lem:spinpull}.  Equip the two products with the corresponding
product spin structures.  We retain these pullback spin structures because
they record the restrictions of the product spin structures on the two ruled
summands; Lemma~\ref{lem:spinframing} then changes only the normal framings.
By that lemma, choose
symplectic normal framings which induce $q_g^*s_g$ and $q_h^*s_h$ on the
two multisections.  The boundary spin structures are then
\[
q_g^*s_g\boxtimes s_{\mathrm{bnd}},\qquad
q_h^*s_h\boxtimes s_{\mathrm{bnd}}.
\]

The group $\operatorname{Sp}(2G,\mathbb Z/2)$ is transitive on quadratic refinements of fixed
Arf invariant \cite{MumfordTheta}.  Reduction
\[
\operatorname{Sp}(2G,\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sp}(2G,\mathbb Z/2)
\]
is onto: the elementary symplectic transvections generating the target
lift integrally.  The mapping class group surjects onto $\operatorname{Sp}(2G,\mathbb Z)$.
Write $\bar q_g$ and $\bar q_h$ for the two pulled-back quadratic
refinements.  Fix an integral symplectic matrix $T_0$ whose mod-two action
satisfies
\[
T_0^*\bar q_h=\bar q_g.
\]
Every matrix in $T_0\Gamma(2)$ has the same mod-two action.
Here
\[
\Gamma(2)=\ker\bigl(\operatorname{Sp}(2G,\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Sp}(2G,\mathbb Z/2)\bigr).
\]

Let $U\subset\operatorname{Sp}(2G,\mathbb R)$ be the locus on which
\[
(Q_{p,g},-Q_{q,h}T)
\]
has rank $2g+2h$.  The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:existence} shows that
$U$ is nonempty and Zariski open.  The subgroup $\Gamma(2)$ has finite
index in $\operatorname{Sp}(2G,\mathbb Z)$ and is therefore Zariski dense.  Hence its
translate $T_0\Gamma(2)$ meets the nonempty Zariski-open set $U$.  Choose a
matrix in the intersection, realize it by a surface diffeomorphism, and
isotope that diffeomorphism to preserve an area form.

Glue this surface map to an orientation-reversing diffeomorphism of the
normal circle.  The surface map identifies the tangential spin
structures.  With the boundary orientations induced from the two
complements, the reversal of the normal circle is exactly the reversal
required by the gluing, and it preserves the bounding spin structure on
$S^1$.  The boundary spin structures therefore match and the complement
spin structures glue.  Hence $w_2(Z)=0$.  Since the chosen
matrix lies in $U$, Mayer--Vietoris gives $H_1(Z;\mathbb Q)=0$.

The free intersection form is even and unimodular, of rank $2k$ and
signature zero.  The indefinite even unimodular lattice of signature
$(k,k)$ is unique \cite[Chapter~II, Sections~4--5]{MilnorHusemoller},
hence it is $kH$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The spin conclusion concerns the closed four-manifold, not merely parity of the free lattice.  When $H_1$ has $2$-torsion, a nonzero $w_2$ can lie in the Ext term and be invisible on $H_2/\operatorname{Tor}$.  The theorem avoids this ambiguity by constructing a genuine spin structure.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:canonical}
Let $Z$ be a spin realization from Theorem~\ref{thm:spin}.  Then
\[
Q_{Z,\mathrm{free}}\cong kH,
\qquad K_\omega^2=4(k+1).
\]
Moreover the image of the symplectic canonical class in $H^2(Z;\mathbb Z)/\operatorname{Tor}$ is characteristic and divisible by two.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
The lattice statement is Theorem~\ref{thm:spin}.  Since $e(Z)=2+2k$ and $\sigma(Z)=0$,
\[
K_\omega^2=2e(Z)+3\sigma(Z)=4(k+1).
\]
The canonical class is characteristic, and on a spin four-manifold its
mod-two reduction is zero.  After passage to the torsion-free quotient,
its image therefore lies in $2(kH)$ and is divisible by two.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:cover}
After fixing the two cyclic characters, identifications of their target
groups, and the standard injections into $\mathbb Z/\ell$, a direct
mixed-sum presentation determines a regular cyclic cover of degree $\ell$.
Over the first complement its inverse image is the disjoint union of $\ell/p$ copies of
\[
\Sigma_G\times P_p,
\]
and over the second complement it is the disjoint union of $\ell/q$ copies of
\[
\Sigma_G\times P_q.
\]
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Define
\[
\beta_p=\frac{\ell}{p}\alpha_p:\pi_1(M_{g,p})\to\mathbb Z/\ell,
\]
and similarly define $\beta_q$.  The restriction of either character to the boundary subgroup is zero: the surface subgroup maps to the kernel of the covering character, and the meridian lies in the punctured-sphere fiber group.  Hence the two characters extend across the amalgamated product to a homomorphism
\[
\beta:\pi_1(Z)\to\mathbb Z/\ell.
\]
Here multiplication by $\ell/p$ means the standard injection
$\mathbb Z/p\hookrightarrow\mathbb Z/\ell$ sending $1$ to $\ell/p$.
The two images have orders $p$ and $q$.  In a cyclic group the subgroup
generated by subgroups of these orders has order
$\operatorname{lcm}(p,q)=\ell$, so $\beta$ is onto.  Its kernel is a
normal subgroup of index $\ell$ and therefore determines a connected
regular cyclic cover with deck group $\mathbb Z/\ell$.  The number of
components over the first complement is
$[\mathbb Z/\ell:\operatorname{im}\beta_p]=\ell/p$, and similarly it is
$\ell/q$ over the second.  Lemma~\ref{lem:productcover} identifies every
component with $\Sigma_G\times P_p$, respectively
$\Sigma_G\times P_q$.  The stated decomposition follows.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
For $k=1$, one has $\ell=n$ in all three numerical cases.  In higher cases the two numbers may differ.  For example, the $k=3$ type $(p,q,n)=(3,3,6)$ has $\ell=3$.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:twisted}
Suppose that a numerical type in Theorem~\ref{thm:classification} is
represented on both nontrivial ruled surfaces by connected unbranched
symplectic multisections $\mathcal A_{g,p}$ and $\mathcal A_{h,q}$ in the
square-zero classes $A_{g,p}$ and $A_{h,q}$.  Then $p$ and $q$ are both
even.  For such a representative,
\[
H_1(E_g\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu \mathcal A_{g,p};\mathbb Z)
\cong \mathbb Z^{2g}\oplus \mathbb Z/(p/2).
\]
Whenever both sides exist as connected unbranched symplectic multisections, a suitable gluing has vanishing rational first homology and hence the rational cohomology ring of $\#_k(S^2\times S^2)$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
The parity restriction follows from the square-zero equation.  Excision
and the Thom isomorphism give the exact segment
\[
H_2(E_g;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow
H_2(E_g,E_g\setminus\nu \mathcal A_{g,p};\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z
\longrightarrow H_1(E_g\setminus\nu \mathcal A_{g,p};\mathbb Z)
\longrightarrow H_1(E_g;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow0.
\]
The first arrow is the intersection map.  Its image is generated by
\[
\gcd\left(p,\frac p2\right)=\frac p2,
\]
the divisibility of $A_{g,p}$.  Since
$H_1(E_g;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^{2g}$ is free, the resulting extension
splits and gives the asserted complement homology.  The finite meridional
term disappears over $\mathbb Q$.  Because the multisections are unbranched,
their covering push-forwards remain surjective with symplectic kernels
over $\mathbb Q$.  The symplectic-position argument of
Theorem~\ref{thm:existence} therefore supplies a gluing for which the
rational Mayer--Vietoris map has full row rank.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
If $p$ is divisible by four, then $A_{g,p}\equiv0\pmod2$.  In the
mod-two pair sequence the kernel of
\[
H^2(E_g;\mathbb Z/2)\longrightarrow
H^2(E_g\setminus\nu \mathcal A_{g,p};\mathbb Z/2)
\]
is generated by $\operatorname{PD}(A_{g,p})$, hence is zero.  The nonzero
$w_2(E_g)$ therefore restricts nontrivially to the complement.  Any mixed
sum containing such a complement is nonspin.  This recovers the behavior
of the twisted degree-four side in the smallest $(2,4)$ construction.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:lowlevels}
At the $k=3$ level there are exactly five unordered numerical types, and at the $k=5$ level there are exactly seven.  Every one of these twelve types admits a minimal equatorially product-framed symplectic realization with the required rational cohomology.  It also admits a spin realization, with free intersection lattice $3H$ for $k=3$ and $5H$ for $k=5$.  None of the direct realizations is simply connected.  For every rational-cohomology realization the first homology is finite.  The persistent quotients $\mathbb Z/p$ and $\mathbb Z/q$ imply that its order is divisible by $\operatorname{lcm}(p,q)$.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
The lists follow from Theorem~\ref{thm:param}.  Existence and minimality are Theorems~\ref{thm:existence} and~\ref{thm:min}; the spin statement is Theorem~\ref{thm:spin}.  Boundary incompressibility gives the nontrivial fundamental group.  By Corollary~\ref{cor:quotients}, a finite first homology group surjects onto both $\mathbb Z/p$ and $\mathbb Z/q$.  Its order is therefore divisible by both $p$ and $q$, and hence by $\operatorname{lcm}(p,q)$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:integralbasis}
For the cyclic cover $\Sigma_G\to\Sigma_g$ determined by a primitive
character, there are symplectic bases
\[
(e_0,f_0),\qquad (e_{i,r},f_{i,r}),\quad 1\leq i\leq g-1,\quad 0\leq r<p,
\]
upstairs and $(a_1,b_1,\ldots,a_g,b_g)$ downstairs such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Qexplicit}
Q_{p,g}(e_0)=pa_1,\qquad Q_{p,g}(f_0)=b_1,
\end{equation}
while
\[
Q_{p,g}(e_{i,r})=a_{i+1},\qquad
Q_{p,g}(f_{i,r})=b_{i+1}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Choose the downstairs basis so that the covering character takes $a_1$
to $1\in\mathbb Z/p$ and vanishes on all other basis elements.  Decompose
$\Sigma_g$ as the union of a once-punctured torus $T$, carrying
$a_1,b_1$, and a genus-$(g-1)$ surface $R$ with one boundary component,
carrying the remaining symplectic pairs.  The induced cover of $T$ is a
connected genus-one surface $\widetilde T$ with $p$ boundary components:
it has Euler characteristic $-p$, its boundary monodromy is trivial, and
the monodromy along $a_1$ is a $p$-cycle.  The inverse image of $R$ is the
disjoint union of $p$ copies $R_0,\ldots,R_{p-1}$.  The closed covering
surface is obtained by gluing the boundary of $R_r$ to the corresponding
boundary component of $\widetilde T$.

Choose a symplectic pair $e_0,f_0$ in the genus-one part of
$\widetilde T$, disjoint from its boundary, so that $e_0$ traverses the
$a_1$ direction through all $p$ sheets and $f_0$ is a lift of $b_1$.
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
e_0\cdot f_0&=1,\\
Q_{p,g}(e_0)&=pa_1,\qquad Q_{p,g}(f_0)=b_1.
\end{aligned}
\]
In each $R_r$, lift the standard symplectic pairs on $R$ and denote them
by $(e_{i,r},f_{i,r})$, $1\leq i\leq g-1$.  Pairs in different $R_r$'s
are disjoint, all of them are disjoint from $e_0,f_0$, and their only
nonzero intersections are
$e_{i,r}\cdot f_{i,r}=1$.  Their push-forwards are
$a_{i+1}$ and $b_{i+1}$, respectively.

Thus the displayed curves have the standard symplectic intersection
matrix and give
\[
1+p(g-1)=G
\]
symplectic pairs, hence $2G$ homology classes.  Since a genus-$G$ surface
has $H_1$ of rank $2G$, the unimodular intersection matrix shows that
these classes form an integral basis.  This proves all the asserted
push-forward formulas.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:k3comparison}
The three $k=3$ model constructions above have the same Euler characteristic, signature, and rational Betti numbers and admit spin realizations with free lattice $3H$, but their mixed-sum presentations have different complement homology and associated cyclic covers.  In particular, the common gluing genus does not determine either the integral complement data or the cyclic-cover decomposition.  No claim is made here that arbitrary closed realizations of the three types are pairwise nondiffeomorphic.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
The numerical invariants and spin statement were established above.  The complement homology groups are respectively
\[
\mathbb Z^4\oplus\mathbb Z/4,
\qquad
\mathbb Z^6\oplus\mathbb Z/3,
\qquad
(\mathbb Z^4\oplus\mathbb Z/6,\ \mathbb Z^8\oplus\mathbb Z/2),
\]
and the cyclic-cover degrees are $4,3,6$.  For the two genus-seven cases, the $(3,3)$ cover has one $\Sigma_7\times P_3$ piece over each side, whereas the $(6,2)$ cover has one $\Sigma_7\times P_6$ piece on one side and three $\Sigma_7\times P_2$ pieces on the other.  This proves the assertion.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:k3lattice}
For each of the three model constructions there is a minimal spin symplectic gluing $Z$ with
\[
H^*(Z;\mathbb Q)\cong H^*(\#_3(S^2\times S^2);\mathbb Q),\qquad
Q_{Z,\mathrm{free}}\cong 3H.
\]
Its fundamental group contains $\pi_1(\Sigma_G)\times\mathbb Z$.  Consequently none of these direct sums is homotopy equivalent to a closed real-hyperbolic four-manifold or to a compact quotient of the bidisk by a torsion-free cocompact irreducible lattice.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Choose the gluing by Theorem~\ref{thm:spin}.  Minimality follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:min}, and the subgroup statement follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:pi1}.  The two lattice exclusions follow from Theorem~\ref{thm:lattice}.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:complexhigher}
Let $Z$ be one of the rational-cohomology higher mixed sums constructed above, with $k>1$, and suppose that $Z$ admits an orientation-compatible complex structure.  Then $Z$ is a minimal surface of general type and
\[
 q(Z)=0,\qquad p_g(Z)=\frac{k-1}{2},\qquad
 c_2(Z)=2(k+1),\qquad K_Z^2=4(k+1),
\]
so that
\[
 K_Z^2=2c_2(Z),\qquad \chi(\mathcal O_Z)=\frac{k+1}{2}.
\]
If $Z$ is a direct mixed sum, its fundamental group is not a torsion-free cocompact irreducible lattice in $\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)\times\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)$.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
The rational cohomology assumption gives $b_1(Z)=0$, $e(Z)=2+2k$, and $\sigma(Z)=0$.  A compact complex surface with even first Betti number is K\"ahler \cite{BHPV}.  The manifolds constructed above are symplectically minimal by Theorem~\ref{thm:min}.  Since $k>1$ gives $b_2^+=k>1$, symplectic minimality is equivalent here to smooth minimality \cite{HamiltonKotschick}.  Therefore the complex surface is minimal as well.

It cannot be rational: a minimal rational surface has $b_2=1$ or $2$, whereas here $b_2=2k>2$.  It cannot be ruled over a positive-genus curve because $b_1=0$.  A minimal K\"ahler surface of Kodaira dimension zero or one has $K^2=0$, whereas
\[
K_Z^2=2e(Z)+3\sigma(Z)=4(k+1)>0.
\]
Thus $Z$ is of general type \cite{BHPV}.  Hodge decomposition gives $q=b_1/2=0$.  Noether's formula gives
\[
\chi(\mathcal O_Z)=\frac{K_Z^2+c_2(Z)}{12}
=\frac{4(k+1)+2(k+1)}{12}=\frac{k+1}{2}.
\]
Since $\chi(\mathcal O_Z)=1-q+p_g$, we obtain $p_g=(k-1)/2$.  The last assertion follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:lattice}.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- question-1: body_md -->
\label{q:smithnormal}
For the five $k=3$ types, and already for the three model cases $(4,4)$, $(3,3)$, and $(6,2)$ studied in detail above, which finite abelian groups occur as $H_1(Z;\mathbb Z)$?  In particular, what are the minimal possible orders in these three cases?  The quotient argument gives the lower divisors
\[
4,\qquad 3,\qquad 6,
\]
for $(4,4)$, $(3,3)$, and $(6,2)$, respectively; determining whether stronger divisibility is forced is part of the Smith-form problem.
<!-- end question-1 -->
<!-- question-2: body_md -->
\label{q:smoothfamilies}
For a fixed odd $k>1$ and a fixed numerical type, are there infinitely many pairwise nondiffeomorphic direct mixed sums with the rational cohomology of $\#_k(S^2\times S^2)$?
<!-- end question-2 -->
<!-- question-3: body_md -->
\label{q:complex}
Do any of the $k=3$ or $k=5$ direct mixed sums admit orientation-compatible complex structures?
<!-- end question-3 -->
